doc.title: Ralph Humphrey interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 11, 2003

title: Giving a clinic and teaching odd meters to students
summary: Humphrey and Rowe discuss the difficulty of presenting complex rhythm in a fifty-minute clinic and how he starts students with hand-to-hand patterns and a bass structure.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Yeah. And it’s got to be a challenge to try to get a fairly complex message across, to me it was anyway, to a room that size, kind of going way back in the room. But I think people gained something from it.
I hope so. I was thinking about that. As I was presenting it I was thinking all right, who is getting any of this, and am I going too fast, there’s too much information, do I leave anything out?
It is difficult. And when I present a subject I usually present it over a period of time rather than squash it into a fifty minute slot.
I had this little picture in my head of trying to do an exercise, maybe with your hands or something that would make you grasp some of those odd meters. Do you ever do that with early students?
Yeah I do that a lot with early students.
Like what kind of things might you do?

Well you know it’s the application can take a number of different approaches but if you’re just talking about like a hand to hand pattern, which is where most guys start, I like to start with creating the bass structure and then relating different ideas to that bass. And what happens at the same time is we’re learning about rhythm, we’re learning about technique, we’re learning about motion, learning about how the body feels when you do something, learning about balance. So there are so many things that are being learned at the same time that you’re doing one thing. I try to show them, reveal to them, all these different levels of learning that’s going on. Because they may not be aware of it. To them it’s just hand to hand. So everything that I do regarding technique usually has some sort © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
of underlying rhythmic element to it that is also being learned, whether it’s, you know, a subtle way or an obvious way.
